subject: Immunology
vignette: A newborn boy is noted to have perioral twitching and carpopedal spasm on day 2 of life. Examination reveals a prominent nose, micrognathia, low-set ears, and a telemetric monitor showing prolonged QT. Echocardiography demonstrates a ventricular septal defect and a truncus arteriosus. Serum calcium is 6.2 mg/dL, and chest radiograph shows no thymic shadow. A fluorescence in situ hybridization study is requested.
question: Which of the following would most likely be seen on FISH testing and on T-cell analysis in this infant?

options.text: Deletion of 22q11.2 with decreased T cells and relatively preserved B cells
Deletion of 22q11.2 with absent B cells and normal T cells
Mutation in RAG1 with absent T and B cells
Mutation in the common gamma chain with absent T and NK cells

explanation_correct: DiGeorge syndrome results from a 22q11.2 deletion, the most common chromosomal microdeletion, and manifests with the CATCH-22 mnemonic: Cardiac defects (truncus arteriosus, tetralogy of Fallot, VSD), Abnormal facies, Thymic hypoplasia, Cleft palate, and Hypocalcemia from parathyroid hypoplasia. Thymic hypoplasia impairs T-cell development, causing decreased T cells and variable cellular immunodeficiency, while B cells are usually normal in number. Severe immunodeficiency requiring thymic transplant occurs only in complete DiGeorge syndrome.

explanation_incorrect.B: Absent B cells with normal T cells describes Bruton agammaglobulinemia, the opposite cell pattern from DiGeorge.
explanation_incorrect.C: RAG1 mutation gives T-B-NK+ SCID presenting with severe infections very early, without the DiGeorge facial or cardiac features.
explanation_incorrect.D: Granulocyte absence (agranulocytosis) is unrelated to 22q11.2 deletion and would cause severe neutropenic sepsis.
explanation_incorrect.E: Common gamma chain mutation is X-linked SCID, which lacks the hypocalcemia, cardiac defects, and parathyroid and facial findings.

educationalObjective: DiGeorge syndrome (22q11.2 deletion) presents with CATCH-22 findings and decreased T cells with normal B-cell numbers due to thymic hypoplasia.

subject: Immunology
vignette: A 2-month-old infant with a known 22q11.2 deletion is admitted with seizures. Laboratory studies show ionized calcium of 0.72 mmol/L, low parathyroid hormone, and a total lymphocyte count of 900/microliter with markedly reduced CD3+ cells. The infant is receiving a live rotavirus vaccine on schedule.
question: Which of the following interventions is most appropriate at this time?

options.text: Administer the live rotavirus vaccine as scheduled
Start lifelong immunoglobulin replacement regardless of antibody levels
Initiate intravenous calcium and vitamin D supplementation while withholding live vaccines

explanation_correct: The hypocalcemia in DiGeorge syndrome arises from parathyroid hypoplasia and requires calcium and active vitamin D repletion, with close monitoring. Because cellular immunity is impaired by thymic hypoplasia, live vaccines should be deferred until the degree of T-cell deficiency is characterized (via CD3 counts and T-cell proliferation), since attenuated organisms can disseminate. Most patients have partial DiGeorge syndrome with only mild immunodeficiency, but complete DiGeorge syndrome may need thymic transplantation.

explanation_incorrect.A: Live vaccines should be postponed in significant T-cell deficiency because of the risk of disseminated vaccine-derived infection.
explanation_incorrect.B: Routine lifelong immunoglobulin is reserved for significant humoral deficiency, not for every patient with DiGeorge syndrome.
explanation_incorrect.D: Corticosteroids suppress T-cell function further and are not a treatment for lymphopenia due to thymic hypoplasia.
explanation_incorrect.E: Splenectomy is indicated for splenic trauma, refractory immune thrombocytopenia, or certain hemolytic anemias, not for DiGeorge syndrome.

educationalObjective: DiGeorge hypocalcemia from parathyroid hypoplasia is treated with calcium and vitamin D, and live vaccines are withheld in significant T-cell deficiency.

subject: Immunology
vignette: A 7-day-old girl with truncus arteriosus undergoes cardiac repair and is found to have profound lymphopenia (absolute lymphocyte count 250/microliter) and absent CD3+ T cells on flow cytometry. She develops severe Pneumocystis pneumonia. Genetic testing confirms a 22q11.2 deletion. Immunologists consider thymic transplantation.
question: Which of the following best explains why this infant has profound deficiency while many other patients with the same deletion have only mild immunodeficiency?

options.text: The deletion is autosomal dominant, so severity is predetermined and uniform
The severity depends on the size of the deletion, and all patients with cardiac defects have complete athymia
Complete DiGeorge syndrome with athymia represents the severe end of a phenotypic spectrum, whereas partial forms retain some thymic tissue
Profound lymphopenia indicates a second, unrelated SCID-causing mutation must always be present
Severe T-cell deficiency is caused by hypocalcemia itself rather than thymic absence

explanation_correct: 22q11.2 deletion has highly variable expressivity. Partial DiGeorge syndrome retains residual thymic tissue and shows varied, usually mild immunodeficiency. Complete DiGeorge syndrome, which occurs in a minority, features athymia with profound T-cell lymphopenia, opportunistic infections such as Pneumocystis pneumonia, and requires thymic transplantation for cure. Cardiac and parathyroid involvement similarly exist on a spectrum, and the deletion is typically de novo, though it can be inherited.

explanation_incorrect.A: 22q11.2 deletion has variable expressivity, and family members with the same deletion can have very different severity, so it is not uniform.
explanation_incorrect.B: Cardiac defects do not reliably predict athymia; many patients with severe cardiac disease have only partial thymic deficiency.
explanation_incorrect.D: A second SCID mutation is not required; complete athymia from the 22q11.2 deletion can itself produce profound lymphopenia.
explanation_incorrect.E: Hypocalcemia results from parathyroid hypoplasia and does not cause lymphopenia, which is due to absent or hypoplastic thymic tissue.

educationalObjective: 22q11.2 deletion has variable expressivity; complete DiGeorge syndrome with athymia is the severe end of the spectrum and requires thymic transplantation.
